topics.name: Coordinate Axes, Coordinate Planes, and Octants
topics.summary: In three dimensions, three mutually perpendicular lines through a fixed origin — the \( x \)-axis, \( y \)-axis, and \( z \)-axis — fix the position of every point by an ordered triple \( (x,y,z) \). Any two axes together determine a coordinate plane (the \( xy \)-, \( yz \)-, or \( zx \)-plane), and the three coordinate planes divide all of space into eight octants, numbered I-VIII by a locked, fixed correspondence with the sign pattern of \( (x,y,z) \) — this numbering never changes and should be memorised rather than re-derived each time. A point lies on a coordinate axis when two of its three coordinates are zero, and on a coordinate plane when exactly one coordinate is zero. The distance of a point from a coordinate axis uses the two coordinates *not* named by that axis (via a two-term square root); the distance from a coordinate plane is simply the absolute value of the one coordinate that plane's name omits — no square root needed. These two formulas are easy to confuse with each other, so always check whether the question asks for an axis or a plane before reaching for a formula.
key_formulas: Distance of \( (x,y,z) \) from the \( x \)-axis: \( \sqrt{y^{2}+z^{2}} \); from the \( y \)-axis: \( \sqrt{x^{2}+z^{2}} \); from the \( z \)-axis: \( \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} \)
Distance of \( (x,y,z) \) from the \( xy \)-plane: \( |z| \); from the \( yz \)-plane: \( |x| \); from the \( zx \)-plane: \( |y| \)
Foot of perpendicular to a coordinate plane: keep the two coordinates naming that plane, set the third to \( 0 \)
Foot of perpendicular to a coordinate axis: keep only the coordinate naming that axis, set the other two to \( 0 \)
topics.worked_example: Find the octant containing \( P(-3,5,-2) \), and its distance from the \( y \)-axis.\nSign pattern of \( P \) is \( (-,+,-) \), which by the locked table is Octant VI. Distance from the \( y \)-axis uses the other two coordinates: \( \sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13} \).
common_mistakes: Confusing the distance-from-an-axis formula (two coordinates, square root) with the distance-from-the-opposite-plane formula (one coordinate, absolute value)
Misreading or swapping the sign of one coordinate when matching a point to its octant
Zeroing the wrong coordinate(s) when finding the foot of a perpendicular to an axis or plane, or zeroing two coordinates instead of one (treating a plane like an axis)
Forgetting that a point can lie on an axis (two zero coordinates) rather than just a plane (one zero coordinate)

topics.name: Distance Between Two Points — Formula and Direct Computation
topics.summary: The distance between two points \( (x_1,y_1,z_1) \) and \( (x_2,y_2,z_2) \) in space is a direct extension of the two-dimensional distance formula: square each of the three coordinate differences, add them, and take the square root. The special case of distance from the origin drops the subtraction entirely, since the origin's coordinates are all zero. The formula's biggest practical hazard is sign-handling: whenever a coordinate being subtracted is itself negative, the subtraction must be written with the negative value in parentheses — \( (5-(-3))^{2} \), never \( (5--3)^{2} \) — otherwise the arithmetic silently goes wrong. This formula underlies almost everything else in the chapter: collinearity and triangle-type checks, quadrilateral classification, and equidistance conditions are all just the distance formula applied two or more times and compared. Word problems (tracking drones, satellites, or survey markers) dress up the same computation in applied language but change nothing about the underlying algebra.
common_mistakes: Dropping the \( z \)-coordinate difference entirely and computing only a two-dimensional distance
Writing a negative coordinate difference without parentheses before squaring, causing a sign error (e.g. treating \( -4^{2} \) as \( -16 \) instead of correctly evaluating \( (-4)^{2}=16 \))
Forgetting to take the final square root after summing the squared differences
In multi-step problems, reusing an intermediate (wrong) point instead of the actually-required one, e.g. finding \( AB \) when the question asks for \( AP \)

topics.name: Distance Formula — Collinearity, Triangles, and Quadrilaterals
topics.summary: The distance formula becomes a powerful diagnostic tool once it is applied to three or four points at once and the resulting side lengths are compared. Three points are collinear exactly when one pairwise distance equals the sum of the other two; otherwise they form a genuine triangle, which can be further classified as scalene (all sides different), isosceles (exactly two sides equal), equilateral (all three equal), or right-angled (the Pythagorean relation holds among the three squared side lengths). Four points, taken in order, form a parallelogram when both pairs of opposite sides are equal; a rhombus additionally requires all four sides equal; and a square additionally requires the two diagonals to be equal as well — note that a genuine square's diagonal is always an irrational multiple of its side (side \( \times\sqrt{2} \)), so diagonals are often left as simplified surds rather than whole numbers. The same machinery also answers equidistance questions: a point equidistant from two others satisfies one distance-squared equation that can be solved directly.
key_formulas: Collinearity test: \( AB+BC=AC \) (or a permutation) \( \Rightarrow A,B,C \) collinear
Right-angle test: for sides \( a\le b\le c \), \( a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2} \Rightarrow \) right-angled, with \( c \) the hypotenuse
Parallelogram \( ABCD \): \( AB=CD \) and \( BC=DA \); rhombus additionally needs \( AB=BC \); square additionally needs \( AC=BD \)
common_mistakes: Checking only one pair of side sums for collinearity instead of confirming which permutation actually works (the largest distance must be the one equal to the sum of the other two)
Concluding a triangle is right-angled without first identifying which side is the longest (the Pythagorean relation only holds relative to the hypotenuse)
Assuming equal diagonals alone (without first confirming equal sides) is enough to prove a square, or expecting a square's diagonal to come out as a whole number
Confusing which two points' midpoints need to coincide when using the diagonals-bisect-each-other property of a parallelogram

topics.name: Section Formula — Internal and External Division
topics.summary: The section formula finds the point that divides the segment joining two given points in a specified ratio \( m:n \). For internal division (the dividing point lies between the two given points), the formula averages the endpoints with weights \( m \) and \( n \) and divides by \( m+n \). For external division (the dividing point lies on the extension of the segment, beyond one of the endpoints), every plus sign in the internal formula becomes a minus sign, including in the denominator — this sign change is the single most common source of error in the whole topic. The same formula runs in reverse too: if a coordinate plane, a specific point, or a stated coordinate value is known to divide a segment somehow, substituting that condition into the section formula and solving recovers the ratio \( m:n \) itself. Midpoint and centroid (covered in the next topic) are simply the special ratio \( 1:1 \) and a three-point analogue of this same idea.
key_formulas: Internal division of \( (x_1,y_1,z_1) \), \( (x_2,y_2,z_2) \) in ratio \( m:n \): \( \left(\frac{mx_2+nx_1}{m+n},\frac{my_2+ny_1}{m+n},\frac{mz_2+nz_1}{m+n}\right) \)
A coordinate plane divides a segment in the ratio found by setting the corresponding coordinate of the internal-division formula to \( 0 \) and solving for \( m:n \)
topics.worked_example: Find the point dividing \( A(2,-1,3) \) and \( B(-4,5,-3) \) internally in the ratio \( 1:2 \).\n\( \left(\frac{1\cdot(-4)+2\cdot 2}{1+2},\frac{1\cdot 5+2\cdot(-1)}{1+2},\frac{1\cdot(-3)+2\cdot 3}{1+2}\right)=\left(\frac{0}{3},\frac{3}{3},\frac{3}{3}\right)=(0,1,1) \).
common_mistakes: Using the internal-division formula (all plus signs) when the question specifies external division, or vice versa
Swapping \( m \) and \( n \), which silently reverses which endpoint the ratio is measured from
Reading off the ratio backwards when reverse-solving — reporting the ratio in which the second point divides, instead of the ratio in which the stated dividing point divides the original segment
Dropping the \( z \)-coordinate calculation and simply copying \( z_1 \) or \( z_2 \) instead of applying the formula to all three coordinates

topics.name: Midpoint, Centroid, and Combined Coordinate-Geometry Applications
topics.summary: The midpoint of a segment and the centroid of a triangle are both simple averages of coordinates: the midpoint averages two endpoints (dividing by \( 2 \)), and the centroid averages three vertices (dividing by \( 3 \)) — mixing up these two divisors is the single most common slip in this topic. Both formulas rearrange cleanly: given a centroid and two vertices, the third vertex can be recovered by isolating it algebraically. These formulas also combine naturally with earlier topics — a midpoint or centroid is just an ordinary point once found, so nothing stops a question from then asking for its octant, its distance from an axis or plane, or its distance from the origin. Word problems in this topic typically involve several tracked objects (drones, survey markers) whose "balanced" or "average" position is exactly the midpoint or centroid computation in applied dress.
key_formulas: Centroid of a triangle with vertices \( (x_1,y_1,z_1),(x_2,y_2,z_2),(x_3,y_3,z_3) \): \( \left(\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3}{3},\frac{y_1+y_2+y_3}{3},\frac{z_1+z_2+z_3}{3}\right) \)
Missing vertex from centroid: \( x_3=3x_G-x_1-x_2 \) (and similarly for \( y_3,z_3 \))
common_mistakes: Dividing by \( 2 \) instead of \( 3 \) when computing a centroid (or vice versa when computing a midpoint), especially after several other formulas in the same problem
Adding the coordinates correctly but forgetting the final division by \( 2 \) or \( 3 \) altogether
Sign errors while isolating a missing vertex from the rearranged centroid formula
Stopping at the midpoint or centroid itself when the question asks a follow-up question about that point (its octant, or its distance from an axis, plane, or the origin)
